keyVerseText: For upon the first day of the first month began he to go up from Babylon, and on the first day of the fifth month came he to Jerusalem, according to the good hand of his God upon him. began: Heb. was the foundation of the going up
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun יְסֻד (yᵉçud) derives from the root verb יָסַד (yâçad), which carries the fundamental sense of establishing, founding, or laying a foundation. This root conveys not only the physical act of setting or founding something but also the figurative establishment of a beginning or a settled foundation. Thus, יְסֻד encapsulates the idea of a foundational starting point or the act of being firmly established, enriching the common English gloss of 'began' with the nuance of a deliberate, stable commencement.
usageInScripture: This word appears once in Scripture, specifically in Ezra 7:9, where it is translated as 'began.' The singular occurrence and its translation as 'began' indicate a focus on the initiation or foundation of an action, in this case, the journey from Babylon to Jerusalem. The consistency in translation underscores the word's role in highlighting the foundational moment or starting point of a significant event, emphasizing the establishment aspect inherent in its meaning.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding יְסֻד as a foundation or beginning rooted in deliberate establishment deepens our appreciation of God's sovereign work in initiating His redemptive plans. It reminds believers that God's actions are not random but founded on His faithful and purposeful will. This word points to the certainty and stability in God's unfolding purposes, encouraging trust in His divine timing and guidance. In Christ, we see the ultimate foundation laid for salvation, making this term a profound reminder that all spiritual journeys and restorations begin with God's firm and gracious initiative.
keyVerseReflection: Ezra 7:9 states, 'For upon the first day of the first month began he to go up from Babylon,' with the Hebrew indicating that this was the 'foundation of the going up.' The use of יְסֻד here highlights that the journey was not merely a casual departure but the established starting point of a divinely guided restoration. This foundation underscores God's providential hand in orchestrating the return to Jerusalem, marking the beginning of a crucial phase in Israel's history and God's redemptive plan.
